G1A01: General licensees are kept out of parts of 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters, which have segments set aside for Advanced and Amateur Extra licensees [97.301(d)]. On 160, 60, 30, 17, 12 and 10 meters a General may use every amateur frequency.
G1A02: The 30-meter band is limited to CW, RTTY and data, so phone is not allowed there [97.305]. 160, 17 and 12 meters all have phone segments.
G1A03: On 30 meters only CW, RTTY and data are authorized, so image modes such as SSTV and fax are prohibited [97.305]. 160, 20 and 12 meters all allow image emissions alongside phone.
G1A05: 7.125 to 7.175 MHz is the Advanced and Extra phone segment of 40 meters, so a General may not transmit there [97.301(d)]. General phone on 40 meters starts at 7.175 MHz, and 28.000 to 28.025 MHz and 21.275 to 21.300 MHz are both open to Generals.
G1A06: A secondary user must not cause harmful interference to primary users and must accept any interference they cause [97.303]. Secondary status does not restrict hours or limit use to emergencies.
G1A07: CW may be sent on any frequency the control operator is authorized to use, and a General has the whole 10-meter band [97.305(a)]. So CW is allowed from 28.000 to 29.700 MHz, not just in the CW and data segment.
G1A08: Only 80, 40, 20 and 15 meters have segments exclusive to Amateur Extra licensees [97.301(b)]. On 160, 60, 30, 17, 12 and 10 meters there are no Extra-only segments.
G1A09: 21300 kHz falls in the General phone segment of 15 meters, 21.275 to 21.450 MHz [97.301(d)]. 14250 kHz is on 20 meters, 18155 kHz on 17 meters and 24900 kHz on 12 meters, so none of them is on 15 meters.
G1A10: Repeaters may not operate on 28.0 to 29.5 MHz, so on 10 meters they are limited to the portion above 29.5 MHz [97.205(b)]. In practice 10-meter FM repeaters sit between 29.5 and 29.7 MHz.
G1A11: Where a General cannot use the whole voice segment, their share is the upper frequency portion [97.301]. The lower end of each phone segment is kept for Advanced and Extra licensees, on 75, 40, 20 and 15 meters alike.
G1B01: An antenna structure more than 200 feet above ground needs FAA notification and FCC registration, even away from airports [97.15(a)]. Near a public use airport a lower structure may need it too.
G1B02: A beacon may not transmit on more than one channel in the same band at the same time from the same station location [97.203(b)]. There is no National Beacon Organization coordination or publication requirement in the rules.
G1B03: The FCC defines a beacon as an amateur station transmitting to observe propagation and reception or for related experiments [97.3(a)(9)]. Repeater identification and bulletins are not beacon purposes.
G1B04: Any amateur station may occasionally retransmit weather and propagation forecasts from US government stations [97.113(c)]. Unidentified test transmissions and encrypted messages are prohibited, and automatic retransmission is limited to repeaters, auxiliary and space stations.
G1B05: One-way transmissions to help people learn Morse code are allowed [97.111(b)(5)]. Unidentified test transmissions are never allowed, and regular broadcasts offering equipment for sale are not a permitted one-way transmission.
G1B06: Under PRB-1, local rules must reasonably accommodate amateur communications and be the minimum practical regulation to serve the local government's legitimate purpose [97.15(b), PRB-1, 101 FCC 2d 952 (1985)]. Localities can regulate, but not unreasonably.
G1B07: Abbreviations and procedural signals are allowed as long as they do not obscure the meaning of the message [97.113(a)(4)]. Q signals are one common kind, but they are not the only ones permitted.
G1B08: US amateurs may contact amateurs in any country except one whose administration has told the ITU it objects to such communications [97.111(a)(1)]. A third-party agreement is needed only to pass messages for third parties, not for ordinary contacts.
G1B09: On HF, an automatically controlled beacon is allowed only on 28.20 to 28.30 MHz [97.203(d)]. Low power or using Morse code does not open up other HF frequencies for automatic beacons.
G1B10: A beacon's transmitter power must not exceed 100 watts [97.203(c)].
G1B11: The FCC decides what counts as good engineering and good amateur practice wherever Part 97 does not spell out a rule [97.101(a)]. The control operator must follow it but does not get to define it.
G1C01: 10.140 MHz is in the 30-meter band, where transmitter output is limited to 200 watts PEP [97.313(c)(1)]. The 1500-watt limit applies on most other HF bands, but not on 30 meters.
G1C02: The 12-meter band has no special limit, so the general maximum of 1500 watts PEP output applies [97.313]. The 100-watt ERP dipole figure is a 60-meter rule.
G1C03: Emissions on 60 meters must not occupy more than 2.8 kHz [97.303(h)(3)]. That allows a normal USB voice or data signal but nothing wider.
G1C04: 60-meter power is set as effective radiated power, so anyone using an antenna other than a dipole must keep the antenna's gain data or calculations in the station records [97.313(i)]. The FCC does not require a full log of contacts on 60 meters.
G1C05: A General may run the full 1500 watts PEP output on 10 meters [97.313]. The 200-watt limit there applies only to Novice and Technician control operators in 28.0 to 28.5 MHz.
G1C06: 160 meters has no special limit, so the maximum of 1500 watts PEP output applies [97.313].
G1C07: A new digital code may be used for RTTY or data as long as its technical characteristics have been publicly documented [97.309(a)(4)]. No type certification, experimental license or rule-making petition is needed.
G1C11: FCC power limits are stated as peak envelope power (PEP) measured at the transmitter output [97.313]. They are not RMS figures and are not measured at the antenna, so feed line loss does not count.
G1D01: Someone who once held a General, Advanced or Amateur Extra license that was not revoked gets credit for the elements it represents, though they must still pass Element 2 [97.501, 97.505(a)]. There is no 5 to 15 year window, and expired Technician licenses from 1987 on earn no credit.
G1D02: A General class VE may administer only Technician exams; General exams need an Advanced or Extra VE and Extra exams an Extra VE [97.509(b)(3)(i)].
G1D03: A CSCE lets a Technician use General privileges right away, on every General or Technician segment, while the upgrade is processed [97.9(b)]. No band is excluded, and there is no waiting for the database or a fee receipt.
G1D04: Every exam needs a team of at least three accredited VEs, and for a Technician exam each must hold General class or higher [97.509(a), (b)(3)(i)]. Technician licensees cannot be VEs.
G1D05: The control operator of a US station needs a US license, wherever they are when operating it by remote control [97.7]. No special remote station permit exists.
G1D06: Until the upgrade appears in the FCC database, a Technician using General frequency privileges must add the indicator AG after the call sign [97.119(f)(2)]. On Technician frequencies no indicator is needed.
G1D07: Volunteer Examiners are accredited by a Volunteer Examiner Coordinator (VEC) [97.509(b)(1)]. The FCC does not accredit individual VEs.
G1D08: Citizenship is not a requirement: a non-US citizen may be a VE if they hold an FCC amateur license of General class or above and meet the other VE rules [97.509(b)(3)]. There is no residence or ITU region test.
G1D09: A CSCE gives credit for the exam elements it shows for 365 days [97.9(b)].
G1D10: A Volunteer Examiner must be at least 18 years old [97.509(b)(2)].
G1D11: After the two-year grace period ends, a former General must prove the old license grant and pass the current Element 2 (Technician) exam; they then get credit for Element 3 [97.505]. Simply showing the expired license is not enough.
G1D12: A station in another country is governed by that country's rules, even when a US operator controls it over the internet [97.507]. FCC rules apply to stations under FCC jurisdiction.
G1E01: A person whose amateur license was revoked and not reinstated may not take part as a third party [97.115(b)(2)]. Citizenship and the language spoken do not disqualify anyone.
G1E02: A 10-meter repeater may retransmit a Technician's 2-meter signal only if the repeater's control operator holds at least a General license, since the repeater is transmitting on a General band [97.205(b)].
G1E03: Outside the automatic control segments, an automatically controlled digital station may only answer an interrogation from a station under local or remote control [97.221]. Two automatic stations may not start a contact there.
G1E04: All listed situations call for specific steps to avoid interference: operating within a mile of an FCC monitoring station, operating on a band where amateurs are secondary, and transmitting spread spectrum [97.13(b), 97.303, 97.311(b)].
G1E05: Messages for a third party in a country with a third-party agreement must relate to amateur radio, be remarks of a personal character, or concern emergencies or disaster relief [97.115(a)(2), 97.117]. No time limit or logging of the third party's name is required.
G1E06: North and South America are in ITU Region 2, whose frequency allocations apply there [97.301, ITU Radio Regulations]. Region 1 covers Europe, Africa and the Middle East, Region 3 most of Asia and the Pacific, and there is no Region 4.
G1E07: Amateur stations may communicate only with other amateur stations, so no part of the 2.4 GHz band may be used to talk with unlicensed Wi-Fi devices [97.111]. Amateurs may share Wi-Fi channel frequencies, but only among licensed hams.
G1E08: Spread spectrum transmissions are limited to 10 watts PEP output [97.313(j)].
G1E10: Those frequencies carry the international propagation beacon network (NCDXF/IARU), so good practice is to keep them clear [97.101]. They are not reserved for emergencies or FCC bulletins.
G1E11: Two automatically controlled digital stations may communicate anywhere RTTY or data is allowed on 6 meters and shorter bands, and in a few small HF segments listed in the rules [97.221, 97.305]. They cannot do so on every digital segment.
G1E12: Third-party messages may be sent by remote control under any circumstances in which the rules allow third-party messages [97.115]. Remote control adds no extra limits beyond the normal third-party rules.
G2A01: By long-standing convention, upper sideband is used for SSB voice on 14 MHz (20 meters) and higher. Lower sideband is the custom only on 160, 75 and 40 meters.
G2A02: Amateurs customarily use lower sideband for voice on 160, 75 and 40 meters. This is a convention, not a rule; above 10 MHz the custom is upper sideband.
G2A03: SSB voice on VHF and UHF follows the same convention as the upper HF bands: upper sideband.
G2A04: 17 and 12 meters are above 14 MHz, so voice there is customarily upper sideband.
G2A05: Single sideband is the usual voice mode on the HF bands because it is narrow and power efficient. FM is mostly used on VHF and UHF, and AM and double sideband are much less common.
G2A06: SSB uses less bandwidth and is more power efficient than AM because no power goes into the carrier or a second sideband. It is not high fidelity and is no better at rejecting static or impulse noise.
G2A07: In SSB only one sideband is sent; the carrier and the other sideband are suppressed. Sending the carrier would make it a different mode, and SSB is not the only voice mode allowed on any band.
G2A08: To break into a phone contact, give your call sign once during a pause. Saying CQ, QRZ or Breaker Breaker is not accepted amateur practice for this.
G2A09: Lower sideband on 160, 75 and 40 meters is simply commonly accepted amateur practice. Either sideband is legal and neither is more efficient on those bands.
G2A10: VOX keys the transmitter when you speak, so you can operate hands free. It does not change audio quality, bandwidth or power output compared with push-to-talk.
G2A11: A station in the lower 48 states calling CQ DX wants contacts from stations outside the contiguous 48 states. Stations inside the lower 48 should not answer.
G2A12: ALC is normally set by adjusting the transmit audio or microphone gain so the meter stays within the recommended range. RF clipping, antenna tuning and the attenuator do not set it.
G2B01: Except during emergencies, no amateur station has priority on any frequency [97.101(b), (c)]. Nets and contacts in progress deserve courtesy, but they have no legal priority.
G2B02: The first step is to acknowledge the station in distress and find out what help it needs. Simply stopping or reducing power does nothing for the person in trouble.
G2B03: If propagation brings in other stations, try to work things out with them in a way that suits everyone. No one has priority, so telling others to leave is not right.
G2B04: Leaving 150 to 500 Hz between CW signals is usually enough to avoid interfering with stations on nearby frequencies. A few tens of hertz is far too close, and kilohertz of space wastes room.
G2B05: An SSB signal is about 2.4 to 3 kHz wide, so leaving 2 to 3 kHz between stations avoids interference. CW-style spacing in hertz would put signals on top of each other.
G2B06: Ask first: send QRL? and your call sign on CW, or on phone ask whether the frequency is in use and give your call sign. Just listening may miss one side of a contact, and QSY means change frequency.
G2B07: Following the voluntary band plan is accepted practice when picking a frequency. Listening for a full two minutes and sending your call three times are not standard requirements.
G2B08: Under the voluntary band plan, stations in the 48 contiguous states use 50.1 to 50.125 MHz only for contacts with stations outside the 48 contiguous states. It is the 6-meter DX window.
G2B09: Only a person holding an FCC-issued amateur operator license may be the control operator of a station transmitting in RACES [97.407(a)]. Government officials without a license may not.
G2B10: Having a backup frequency in case of interference or poor conditions is good net management. Reading the whole roster every session or using several sets of phonetics only wastes time.
G2B11: RACES training drills and tests may total no more than 1 hour per week without special approval [97.407(d)(4)]. Longer exercises need approval from the state's chief emergency planning officer.
G2C01: With full break-in (QSK), the transmitting station can hear between dots, dashes and characters, so the other operator can break in at any moment. It has nothing to do with keyers or manual switches.
G2C02: QRS? means "Shall I send more slowly?", and the request is to send slower. Changing frequency or power is not what it asks for.
G2C03: KN at the end of a transmission means go ahead, but only the station or stations already in contact should reply. Others should not call in.
G2C04: QRL? asks "Are you busy?" or "Is this frequency in use?" It is the standard check before calling on a frequency.
G2C05: Answer at the fastest speed you can copy comfortably, but never faster than the station calling CQ. There is no standard calling speed.
G2C06: Zero beat means setting your transmit frequency to match the received signal, so both stations are on the same frequency. It has nothing to do with speed or accuracy.
G2C07: A C after the RST report means the signal is chirpy or unstable in frequency. Key clicks are reported with a K.
G2C08: AR marks the end of a formal message in CW. SK means the end of contact, BK means break, and KN means only the named station should reply.
G2C09: QSL means "I have received and understood" (acknowledgment of receipt). That is also why confirmation cards are called QSL cards.
G2C10: QRN means "I am troubled by static" (natural noise). Man-made interference is QRM, and send more slowly is QRS.
G2C11: QRV means "I am ready (to receive)". Sending too fast is QRS and interference is QRM.
G2D01: The Volunteer Monitor Program is a group of amateur volunteers formally enlisted to monitor the bands for rule violations. VEs run exams and frequency coordinators handle repeaters, which are separate roles.
G2D02: The Volunteer Monitor Program aims to encourage amateurs to self-regulate and follow the rules. It does not run exams, coordinate repeaters or provide emergency communications.
G2D03: Monitors take beam headings on the repeater input from their own locations and compare them; where the bearings cross is the likely source. Comparing input and output strength cannot locate the station.
G2D04: An azimuthal projection map is centered on one location and shows true bearings and distances from it, so you can aim a beam at a distant station. It distorts the shape of land masses.
G2D05: A general call is CQ a few times, then "this is" and your call sign a few times, then listen, repeating as needed. QTC concerns messages, and an unmodulated carrier is not a call.
G2D06: For a long-path contact you point the antenna 180 degrees from the short-path heading, so the signal goes the long way around the earth.
G2D07: Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, Delta are the NATO (ITU) phonetic alphabet. Able, Baker, Charlie, Dog is an older military alphabet that is no longer standard.
G2D08: The FCC no longer requires a general station log, but keeping one helps you answer if the FCC asks about your station's operation. License renewal needs no evidence of operation.
G2D09: The only requirement in a contest is to identify your station as FCC rules require. Submitting a log and sending QSL cards are optional.
G2D10: QRP means low-power operation, commonly 5 watts or less on CW. It is not a remote control or relay procedure.
G2D11: Early signal reports tell each station how well it is being heard, so both can adjust speed, power or procedure to the conditions. They are not needed for awards or frequency calibration.
G2E01: When AFSK RTTY is sent through an SSB transmitter, LSB is the convention, so the mark and space tones come out in the standard orientation.
G2E02: VARA is a digital protocol (a sound card modem) used with Winlink to move email over radio. It is not a moonbounce mode or a direction-finding system.
G2E03: Interference to a PACTOR or VARA link can cause all of the listed problems: frequent retries or timeouts, long pauses in transfer, and failure to connect at all.
G2E04: In FT8 you transmit in the time slot opposite the calling station, on a clear audio frequency. Calling on the station's own frequency or in the same slot means you transmit while it does.
G2E05: JT65, JT9, FT4 and FT8 are sent with upper sideband when using audio tones (AFSK). That is the convention on every band.
G2E06: The usual shift for amateur RTTY on HF is 170 Hz. 850 Hz was used in older equipment and 425 Hz is not common.
G2E07: FT8 needs the computer clock accurate to within about 1 second, since transmissions are timed in fixed 15-second slots. Ordinary sound card interfaces work, and no special antenna is needed.
G2E08: Most 20-meter digital activity is between 14.070 and 14.100 MHz, below the beacon frequency at 14.100 MHz. The SSB and SSTV areas are higher in the band.
G2E09: PACTOR connections are between two stations only, so you cannot join an existing contact. Transmitting a carrier to break it would be deliberate interference.
G2E10: To reach a digital messaging gateway, transmit a connect request on its published frequency. Sending an email or QRL does not open a radio link.
G2E11: AREDN mesh networks provide high-speed data services, such as networking, video and voice, for emergencies and community events. They are not repeater coverage or DX spotting systems.
G2E12: All listed statements describe Winlink: it sends and receives internet email over amateur radio, it can use packet radio, and it works on both VHF and HF.
G2E13: A Winlink Remote Message Server is also called a gateway, because it links radio users to the Winlink email system. A TNC is a modem, not a server.
G2E14: Any of the listed problems can stop an FSK decode: reversed mark and space, the wrong baud rate, or the wrong sideband, which also reverses the tones.
G2E15: FT8 on 20 meters is commonly found around 14.074 MHz, using about 3 kHz up to roughly 14.077 MHz. The voice and CW areas are not where FT8 is usually run.
